segments.text: Subqueries: a query inside a query.
Which grades are above the average? A subquery is like asking a colleague for that figure before you finish your own report.
The inner query, in brackets, runs first. The average of the six grades is seven point two five, and that one value takes its place.
Three grades beat it: nine, eight point five and seven point five.
When a subquery returns a list, use IN. Think of the guest list at a party door: is your id on the list?
Python has two students, so the query returns Luis Gil and Eva Sanz.
With an equals sign, a list makes Oracle fail with error zero one four two seven. Use IN.
ANY and ALL compare a value with a whole list. Take the Databases grades: five, six point five and eight point five.
Greater than ALL means greater than every one, so above the largest, eight point five. Only the nine in Python passes.
Greater than ANY means greater than at least one, so above the smallest, five. All three grades of the other courses pass.
Now a trap. NOT IN keeps the grades that are not in the list. Python's grades are nine and seven point five, so four rows come back.
Add one Python enrolment without a grade, and the list now holds a NULL. Suddenly, no rows at all.
NOT IN means different from every value, and different from NULL is unknown, never true. So nothing passes.
Filter out the NULLs, or use NOT EXISTS.
A correlated subquery uses a column of the outer query. Like a tutor opening each student's file, it runs again for every outer row.
For each enrolment, it finds the best grade of that row's course, and keeps the row if its grade is equal.
The result: the top student of each course. A tie would return several rows.
EXISTS asks a yes or no question: does the subquery find at least one row? What it selects does not matter, so people write SELECT 1.
Databases, Python and Statistics all have enrolments. Marketing has none, so NOT EXISTS returns just Marketing.
And unlike NOT IN, it is not fooled by NULLs.
A subquery in FROM is an inline view: a temporary table you can query, with an alias. In Oracle, no AS before that alias.
Here it computes the average per course: six point six seven for Databases, eight point two five for Python, and seven for Statistics.
Then we join it to course and keep the averages of seven or more: Python and Statistics.
Practise it in the SQL section of the course site.
